issues.title: Step-up authentication has no carrier at the token endpoint
issues.author: ogazitt
issues.body:
A PDP that denies because the subject authenticated too weakly knows something
the client could act on: which `acr` and `amr` values would have permitted the
request. Neither end of that is specified today.

- AuthZEN carries `acr_values` / `amr_values` only in the **non-normative
  example** of Section 5.5.2.3. The keys are never defined, so there is
  nothing normative for this profile to reference.
- `insufficient_user_authentication` (RFC 9470) is defined for resource
  servers. The token endpoint has no equivalent.

The Error Mapping section currently says an AS SHOULD surface the requirement
and declines to define how.

Closing this needs work in both specifications, which is why it may deserve
its own document rather than a paragraph here. The AuthZEN half should be
raised with the AuthZEN WG.

issues.title: No error code is named for a policy denial
issues.author: ogazitt
issues.body:
The Error Mapping table says "fail the request; do not issue" for a gate
denial without naming an OAuth error code. That reflects the state of the
neighbouring specifications, which have no consensus:

- **RFC 8693** Section 2.2.1 says the AS MUST use `invalid_request` when a
  token is "unacceptable based on policy" - which contradicts RFC 6749
  Section 5.2, where `invalid_request` means the request is *malformed*.
- **Identity chaining** defers to RFC 7523 Section 3.1, i.e. `invalid_grant`.
- **ID-JAG** and **Transaction Tokens** describe policy denial in detail and
  name no error code at all.
- `access_denied` is semantically exact ("the resource owner or authorization
  server denied the request") but is defined at the authorization endpoint in
  RFC 6749 Section 4.1.2.1. RFC 8628 Section 3.5 does use it at the token
  endpoint, which weakens that objection.

Should this profile name a code, or stay silent deliberately, so that a client
cannot infer which gate failed?

issues.title: A partial grant has no signal beyond the scope parameter
issues.author: ogazitt
issues.body:
A scope tuple denial narrows the issued token rather than failing the request.
The scope case is covered: RFC 6749 Section 5.1 and RFC 8693 Section 2.2.1
require the `scope` response parameter when the granted scope differs from the
requested scope, and ID-JAG states that granted scopes may be a subset of
those requested.

Nothing covers the rest of it. There is no signal for a narrowed `audience` or
for filtered `authorization_details`, and nothing conveys *why* a privilege
was dropped. A client that asked for three scopes and got two cannot tell
whether the third was refused by policy or was never recognized.

Related to #2, which is the same gap seen from the failure side.

issues.title: Which URN namespace names the capability
issues.author: ogazitt
issues.body:
Section 12.1 sets out three resolutions and leaves the choice to the working
group:

1. This document (or a companion) performs the RFC 3553 registration of the
   `authzen` sub-namespace of `urn:ietf:params`, satisfying the IETF Review
   policy that AuthZEN 1.0 Section 12 asks for and that a specification
   published outside the IETF stream cannot satisfy on its own.
2. Name the capability under `urn:openid:authzen` instead, requesting no IANA
   action. ARAP already does this, so it is the scheme AuthZEN profiles use in
   practice.
3. Decline the dependency and register under `urn:ietf:params:oauth`
   (RFC 6755), whose Specification Required policy is not blocked.

A capability identifier is only useful if both parties compute the same
string, so one scheme for all AuthZEN capabilities is worth more than this
document's independence from any of them. Options 1 and 2 both achieve that
and differ only in which body assigns the name.

Needs to be settled jointly with the AuthZEN WG rather than here alone.

issues.title: Is a new registry the right way to name gate actions?
issues.author: ogazitt
issues.body:
The gate action name is `issue:<token-type>:<grant-type>`, composed from short
names held in two registries this document creates, rather than from the
existing OAuth grant type URIs.

The reason is portability: relation identifiers in real policy engines have
length and character constraints that the URIs exceed, so a composed name
built from URIs could not be carried into a relationship-based engine without
rewriting the policy.

The counter-argument is that inventing a parallel vocabulary for grants that
already have registered identifiers is a cost of its own, and that engines
could canonicalize instead. This is the kind of naming call the working group
is better placed to make.

issues.title: Batch size, latency budget and caching are unspecified
issues.author: ogazitt
issues.body:
A request naming several scopes against several audiences produces a cross
product of evaluations. Section 4.1 addresses colocation and the latency
argument, but the document says nothing about:

- an upper bound on the number of evaluations in one batch, or pagination
- the latency budget an AS should assume on the token path
- whether, and for how long, a decision may be cached

The third is the one with security consequences, since caching a permit is
the thing the whole framework is arguing against doing in a token.

issues.title: Fail closed, but with what response?
issues.author: ogazitt
issues.body:
The draft says that an unreachable PDP, or a malformed decision response,
means the AS fails closed and does not issue. It does not say what the client
sees.

RFC 6749 has no token endpoint equivalent of a 503. HTTP 503 with `Retry-After`
may be sufficient on its own, or `temporarily_unavailable` semantics may need
defining for this endpoint.

This interacts with `I-D.gerber-oauth-deferred-token-response` (cited in
Section 4.2 as the escape hatch for decisions that cannot be made
synchronously): a PDP that is merely slow and a PDP that is down should
probably not look the same to a client.

issues.title: Two smaller questions on the response vocabulary
issues.author: ogazitt
issues.body:
Both carried forward from the analysis that produced Section 6, neither
blocking.

**Refresh token lifetime.** Should `token_lifetime` have a companion key for
the refresh token, or is refresh issuance simply a separate decision with its
own evaluation? The latter is cleaner but means an AS cannot express "issue
this access token, but no refresh token" in a single call.

**Response signing with `crit`.** Should signing the decision response be
REQUIRED when `crit` is used? Leaning no, on the grounds that an attacker who
can strip `crit` can equally flip `decision` to `true`, so `crit` adds no
attack surface that transport security does not already have to cover. A
security area reviewer will ask, so the reasoning should probably be written
down either way.

issues.title: Requested authorization_details are not represented in the evaluation request
issues.author: mcguinness
issues.body:
**Document:** `draft-gazitt-oauth-authzen-issuance.md` (AuthZEN Profile for OAuth 2.0 Token Issuance). References use heading anchors, since section numbering is generated.

Forming the Evaluation Request (`#request`) surfaces the three request inputs to the PDP three different ways, and `authorization_details` is the odd one out:

- **Scopes**: one scope tuple per requested scope, `action.name` set to the scope value verbatim (Scope Tuple, `#scope-tuple`), decided per item under `execute_all` (Batching and Result Composition, `#composition`).
- **Resource indicators**: the RFC 8707 `resource` (or `audience`) parameter determines a single shared `resource.id` (Resource).
- **`authorization_details`**: no request-side representation. Processing the Evaluation Response (`#shaping`) defines the `authorization_details` constraining key (replace not merge, structural subset per RFC 9396), but nothing carries the *requested* RAR into the evaluation request. The request-construction sections (Subject, Resource, Actions, Context, Batching) never mention it.

**Consequence:** the PDP is required to narrow `authorization_details` and return a subset without ever receiving the requested details in the structured request. They have to be conveyed out of band, which is the shared evaluation-request construction that Related Work (`#related`) already flags as expected alignment work. It is also asymmetric with scopes (which get a real per-item decision), and it is an interop gap, since two PDPs behind one AS have no defined view of the requested RAR.

**Options:**

1. Per-detail tuple, analogous to the scope tuple. One evaluation per requested `authorization_detail`, decided under `execute_all`.
2. Request-side context key carrying the requested `authorization_details` array, so the PDP sees them when computing the shaping key.
3. Status quo, with explicit text that requested `authorization_details` are out of scope of the evaluation request and conveyed by deployment agreement.

A weaker version of the same gap applies to resource indicators: a single `resource.id` on the shared evaluation cannot express multiple requested resources with per-resource narrowing, so `audience` narrows without a per-resource decision.

**Related:** #3 is the response-side counterpart (signalling a partial grant). This issue is the request side, that the PDP never receives the requested `authorization_details` to decide on. Also affects `draft-gazitt-oauth-authzen-token-exchange.md`, which reuses this document's response processing including the `authorization_details` key.

comments.author: ogazitt
comments.body:
Thanks @mcguinness, I agree that the current draft is weak on how rich authorization requests are decomposed into AuthZEN evaluations. I'll think about this more.

Of course, I'll also consider the other points.

comments.author: ogazitt
comments.body:
@mcguinness Confirmed - this is a real gap. `authorization_details` shows up as a
constraining key in 6.4.4 and nowhere in 5, so the PDP is being asked to
narrow an input it never sees.

One correction to the framing. The structural check in 6.4.4 binds the AS,
not the PDP:

> Every returned entry MUST have a `type` present in the request ... The AS
> MUST reject the decision otherwise.

The AS has the request. A PDP returning entries nobody asked for gets its
decision rejected, so the fail-closed path holds and this is a functionality
gap rather than a security one. Your interop point survives that intact: two
PDPs behind one AS still have no defined view of the request, and nothing
makes them agree on what a `payment_initiation` entry means.

Of your three options: I think 2 is the wrong shape, and 1 is pointing in the
right direction but stops one level too early.

Option 2 puts the input the whole decision turns on into `context`, which 5.4
defines as advisory. A PDP may ignore it and a policy author has no guarantee
it arrives. The profile pushes decision-critical inputs into the five-tuple
everywhere else, and I would rather not make RAR the exception.

Option 1 has the right instinct - the entry belongs in the tuple, not in a
property bag - but one evaluation per whole entry only buys entry-level
filtering, and 6.4.4 already permits narrowing *within* an entry: dropping a
location, dropping an action. A per-entry boolean cannot express that. It also
leaves you with no natural `action.name`.

So I want to take option 1 further and decompose the entry along the seams RFC
9396 already gives it:

| RAR member | AuthZEN |
|---|---|
| `type` | `resource.type` |
| each `locations` entry | `resource.id` |
| each `actions` entry | `action.name` |

One evaluation per (location, action) pair, batched under `execute_all`, with
the AS reassembling the permitted pairs into narrowed entries. Same shape as
the scope tuple in 5.3.3, composed the same way in 5.5.

For the RFC 9396 payment example:

```json
{
  "type": "payment_initiation",
  "locations": ["https://example.com/payments"],
  "actions": ["initiate", "status"],
  "instructedAmount": { "currency": "EUR", "amount": "123.50" }
}
```

the request is the gate tuple plus one tuple per pair, in the shape 9.1
already uses:

```json
{
  "subject":  { "type": "user", "id": "U0405936" },
  "resource": { "type": "audience", "id": "https://bank.example" },
  "context": {
    "client_id": "pisp-app",
    "acr": "urn:example:loa:3",
    "issuance": {
      "capabilities": [
        "urn:ietf:params:authzen:token-issuance"
      ],
      "authorization_details": [
        {
          "type": "payment_initiation",
          "instructedAmount": { "currency": "EUR", "amount": "123.50" }
        }
      ]
    }
  },
  "evaluations": [
    { "action": { "name": "issue:access_token:authorization_code" } },
    {
      "action":   { "name": "initiate" },
      "resource": { "type": "payment_initiation",
                    "id": "https://example.com/payments" }
    },
    {
      "action":   { "name": "status" },
      "resource": { "type": "payment_initiation",
                    "id": "https://example.com/payments" }
    }
  ],
  "options": { "evaluations_semantic": "execute_all" }
}
```

If the gate passes and only `status` is permitted, the AS returns the entry
with `actions` narrowed to `["status"]`. The subset rule in 6.4.4 stops being
something the AS has to police after the fact and becomes a property of how
the request was built.

Note what is and is not in `context` there. The decomposable members are
tuples, so the decision does not depend on the property bag - that is the
difference from option 2. What stays in `context` is `instructedAmount`, which
does not decompose onto a tuple and which 1.2 already handles by name: "a
payment amount, a rate limit - those flow in as advisory context and out as
token shaping." A PDP that ignores it still adjudicates the gate and the
(location, action) pairs correctly; one that reads it can also cap the amount.

Two things this costs.

First, it needs per-evaluation resource overrides, and 5.2 currently says
`resource.type` MUST be `audience` with a single shared `resource.id`. The
Evaluations API allows the override, as above; my text forbids it. That MUST
has to loosen. Your resource-indicator point is the same constraint from the
other direction, so I split it out as #10 - both want the same fix and I would
rather decide them together.

Second, 1.2 states that advisory-context rule generally, about deployments
rather than about RAR, so today it only covers `instructedAmount` by
implication. And `datatypes` has no home at all yet. The `-01` text needs to
be explicit about both.

I would rather write this as a section of `-01` than a separate binding
document.

Does the decomposition hold up against the RAR types you have in mind? The
case I want to hear about is one where the (location, action) product is the
wrong unit of decision.

issues.title: Resource section assumes a single issuance target; RFC 8707 permits several
issues.author: ogazitt
issues.body:
Split out from #9, where @mcguinness raised it as a sub-point.

5.2 says:

> `resource.type` MUST be `audience`. `resource.id` MUST be the issuance target.
> Where the request carries an explicit target - an `audience` parameter, or a
> `resource` parameter in the sense of {{RFC8707}} - that value determines
> `resource.id`.

Singular throughout. But RFC 8707 §2 permits the `resource` parameter to appear multiple times, and RFC 8693 §2.1 does the same for `audience` and `resource` in a token exchange request. A request for three resource indicators has three issuance targets, and 5.2 gives no way to express that.

6.4.3 already assumes the plural case on the response side:

> Each value MUST appear among the `resource.id` values of the permitted evaluations.

`resource.id` values, plural, across evaluations. So the response key is written to narrow a set that the request-construction rules can only ever populate with one member. The narrowing is unreachable.

The fix is presumably one evaluation per resource indicator, batched under `execute_all` the way scope tuples already are in 5.3.3, with 5.5 composing the permitted targets. That needs per-evaluation resource overrides, which the Evaluations API allows but 5.2's MUST currently forbids - the same constraint that #9 runs into.

Worth deciding both at once, since they loosen the same rule.

issues.title: Related Work should cite Grant Management for OAuth 2.0
issues.author: ogazitt
issues.body:
**Document:** `draft-gazitt-oauth-authzen-issuance.md`, Related Work (`#related`).

Grant Management for OAuth 2.0 (OIDF FAPI WG, `oauth-v2-grant-management-03`, 9 May 2023) defines a grant query response whose members are `scopes`, `claims`, `authorization_details` and `expires_at`.

That is this document's constraining and decorating key set. Same vocabulary, two moments in a grant's life: this document specifies how a Policy Decision Point shapes a grant at issuance, Grant Management specifies how a client reads it back afterwards.

Its `scopes` entries are also `{scope, resource}` pairs, where `resource` is an array of RFC 8707 resource indicators, which is convergent support for #10.

**Action:** add a Related Work paragraph in `-01`. No normative effect.

issues.title: crit: §6 MUST NOT contradicts the §8 rationale and disarms crit against undeclared ASes
issues.author: ogazitt
issues.body:
Two normative statements in the draft cannot both hold.

**§6, in the definition of `crit`:**

> A PDP MUST NOT include `crit` unless the AS has declared support for the corresponding capability (§8).

**§8, Policy Enforcement Point Capabilities:**

> The declaration is an optimization, not a safety mechanism, and this is why it is OPTIONAL. Safety is already unilateral: a PDP that marks a key `crit` obliges any AS implementing this profile to fail closed if it does not understand it (§5.1), and an AS that does not implement this profile ignores the `issuance` envelope entirely, `crit` included. Withholding `crit` from an undeclared AS therefore protects nothing.

The second paragraph argues that withholding `crit` from an undeclared AS accomplishes nothing. The first paragraph then requires exactly that, as a MUST NOT.

## Why this is a real problem and not just untidy prose

The declaration is OPTIONAL. So there is a conforming population of authorization servers that implement this profile, would honour `crit` correctly under the mandatory-to-understand rule in §5.1, and simply never sent a capability declaration because §8 told them it was an optimization they could skip.

Against that population the §6 MUST NOT forbids a PDP from marking any key `crit`. The mechanism whose entire purpose is to prevent a silent broadening of the grant is disabled for implementations that declined an optimization. That is the opposite of failing safe, and §8 already says the withholding buys nothing in exchange.

It also diverges from the mechanism the name was borrowed from. `crit` in RFC 7515 §4.1.11 is unilateral: the producer marks a header critical and a recipient that does not understand it MUST reject the JWS. There is no handshake and no precondition on the producer.

## Resolutions, in the order I currently prefer them

1. **Drop the §6 MUST NOT.** `crit` becomes unilateral, matching RFC 7515, matching the §5.1 rule, and matching the reasoning already written in §8. The capability declaration stays OPTIONAL and stays an optimization: a PDP that knows what the AS supports can choose a decision the AS can actually enforce, which is the benefit §8 claims for it.
2. **Downgrade to SHOULD NOT.** A PDP that has a declaration in hand and can see the capability is absent has a good reason not to send `crit`, since the permit will just turn into a denial. But absence of a declaration is not evidence of absence of support, so it should not be a hard bar.
3. **Make the declaration REQUIRED and keep the MUST NOT.** Internally consistent, but it contradicts the §8 rationale outright, adds a mandatory round trip to every deployment including those using only the keys defined here, and makes the profile harder to adopt incrementally.

## Interaction with the AuthZEN extensibility work

Karl McGuinness has proposed a `mandatory_extensions` signal by which a PEP asserts it will fail closed on named extensions, discussed on the WG mailing list on 2026-08-12 and on the agenda for the next call. That proposal is a generalized form of resolution 3, lifted out of this profile and into AuthZEN itself.

Worth noting that the two mechanisms are not substitutes. `mandatory_extensions` would be per-request and static, declaring what the PEP is prepared to honour. `crit` is per-response and dynamic, naming which keys in this particular decision must be honoured. A general extensibility signal would be the precondition for `crit` rather than a replacement for it, so this issue needs resolving on its own terms whichever way that work goes.

## Related

There is a second, separate problem with where the declaration lives, which will get its own issue: the declaration sits in `context`, and AuthZEN 1.0 specifies that a `context` supplied inside an individual evaluation object overrides the top-level default rather than merging with it.

issues.title: No way to correlate a PDP decision with the token the AS mints
issues.author: ogazitt
issues.body:
Raised by Michael Schwartz (Gluu) on the OpenID AuthZEN mailing list,
2026-08-13:

> If you proceed with this for some reason, please ensure you send the token's
> jti so we can correlate it in the logs.

[Message 689](https://lists.openid.net/pipermail/openid-specs-authzen/2026-August/000689.html)

An operator running an AS and a PDP has two decision logs and no defined way to
join them. The draft says nothing about correlation: `jti` appears only in the
§5.4 provenance table, as a claim the PDP does not get to set, and there is no
correlation identifier anywhere in the request direction.

The obvious fix - send the `jti` - has an ordering problem. At evaluation time
the token has not been minted, so there is no `jti` yet. An AS would have to
pre-allocate the identifier before the decision, and on a deny it would burn an
identifier for a token that is never issued. Pre-allocation is workable but it
is a real constraint on AS implementations and should not be assumed silently.

Options:

1. **Require the AS to pre-allocate `jti` and send it** in the evaluation
   request context. Strongest join, highest implementation cost, awkward on
   deny.
2. **Define a separate request correlation identifier** that the AS also
   records against the eventual `jti` in its own log. Cheap, no ordering
   problem, works on deny, but the join needs both logs.
3. **Say nothing normative and note it as an operational consideration.**

Preference is (2), possibly with (1) as a MAY where the AS already
pre-allocates. Whichever way it lands, the Security or Operational
Considerations should say something, since today the answer is silence.

Applies to both `draft-gazitt-oauth-authzen-issuance` and
`draft-gazitt-oauth-authzen-token-exchange`, and to the claim enrichment call
in `draft-gazitt-oauth-authzen-claims`.

comments.author: ogazitt
comments.body:
Resolved as **option 1, as a `MAY`**, in 5fe6950.

`jti` is now a context key on the evaluation request, and §5.4.1 Correlation
explains when to send it:

https://ogazitt.github.io/oauth-authzen/draft-gazitt-oauth-authzen-issuance.html#name-correlation

An AS MAY include in `context` the `jti` of the token it intends to mint, so
that the record the PDP writes and the token the AS issues carry the same
identifier.

It is a `MAY` rather than a `SHOULD` because of the ordering problem this issue
raised. The text names it and then hands it to the implementer: whether to
pre-allocate, and what to do with an identifier spent on a denial, is an
implementation matter for the AS and is outside the scope of the document. An
AS that does not pre-allocate omits the key and pays nothing for the feature.
The text also states that supplying `jti` as an input does not disturb the §6.5
reservation - the AS remains authoritative for the claim, and a PDP still MUST
NOT set it in the response.

**Option 2 is rejected.** This issue stated a preference for a separate
correlation identifier that the AS would record against the eventual `jti` in
its own log. Michael Schwartz, who raised the original request, asked for
option 1 as a MAY instead, in
[message 691](https://lists.openid.net/pipermail/openid-specs-authzen/2026-August/000691.html):

> my preference is optional "jti" and leave it up to the IDP to figure out how
> to correlate that with the actual token.

That is the better answer. A second identifier is a new thing for both sides to
carry and to join on, in service of a case that option 1 already covers
whenever the AS can pre-allocate. Sending the real identifier when you have one
is cheaper for everybody.

The accepted cost is that correlation is best-effort: an operator running an AS
that cannot pre-allocate gets no join from this specification. That is the price
of imposing nothing on such an AS, and it is the right trade for a key on an
advisory context object.

No change is needed in the companion drafts. `draft-gazitt-oauth-authzen-token-exchange`
inherits context keys from the framework, and `draft-gazitt-oauth-authzen-claims`
already directs the AS to convey the same context values on a search.

Thanks to Michael Schwartz (Gluu) for raising it.
